Catastrophic failure is unlikely. 12 gauge chamber is larger than a .50 chamber, their mouths are approximately the same diameter which is what permits the above image, however a 12 gauge chamber does not taper off like a .50. Also, a .50 projectile is too small to form a seal with a 12 gauge bore, allowing gas to escape out the barrel immediately instead of having to push against the projectile. Additionally, due to a lack of seal between the projectile and bore, the gas will immediately start pushing unburnt powder down the barrel, faster than if the cartridge was in a proper .50 chamber and thus would have to push the round out of the way first before hand, resulting in most of the powder burning outside of the chamber, reducing the pressure applied at any one point. In fact, I believe most of the powder will not burn at all, and simply be ejected out the barrel along with the projectile (assuming it doesn't keyhole and squib itself inside the barrel). All of these factors combined reduce chamber pressure enough to likely avoid catastrophic failure.

Catastrophic failure may still be possible, the burn rate of the powder may increase chamber pressure faster than it can bleed off by escaping down the barrel and possibly exceed the chamber's tolerances, I would have to do some calculations to confirm or deny that, however I find it unlikely. Out of battery fire due to improper head-spacing, or damage to the barrel due to the projectile key-holing are more likely than catastrophic failure of the chamber.
